The second speaker, by addressing fears of the first speaker, seems to be attempting to reduce uncertainty. However, the reduction of uncertainty appears to have the opposite effect in that a second speaker who does not address uncertainties does not reduce uncertainty and therefore is perceived as a higher - not lower - authority. Person 1, who may have been expressing doubts about his/her authority in the first turn, gains authority. This is apparent from the fact that person 1 does not address the authority issue, person 2 addresses the person's doubts but also reduces doubts, and person 2 appears to have a level of higher authority. This is further evidence that the speaker who addresses the person's doubt may have a lower level of authority than the speaker who does not. We don't usually use the word 'today' to talk about days of the week in American English. We say Monday, Tuesday, etc. Sometimes we do say Tuesday, July 12, but we often just say July 12th.
In the conversation above, notice the use of words like: tomorrow, this afternoon, early, etc.
The reason why we say 'today' instead of 'Tuesday' is because today is the most important part of the sentence. We might talk about other things before today but today is most important. If it was Tuesday, we might talk about Monday and say we have Wednesday and it would not be important.

3. Don't burn bridges.
After you quit, you may still need to work with your boss or coworkers on projects. Or you may need to use your previous company for references. So don't burn any bridges.
4. Be polite.

How do I show sympathy in English or compassion?
—
We usually show sympathy in the way we talk to people, our body language and facial expressions.
—
I don't think you are going to lose your job. = I don't believe you are going to lose your job.
—
We can use "You're going to lose your job." in informal conversation to show sympathy.
In a face to face conversation, you can also show you are concerned about someone by looking at them very closely, in other words, staring.
Note: this word is not suitable for use with children or people you do not know. In those situations, we typically say:
Are you okay? You don't look alright.
—
We can also show sympathy in writing as well, for example we can use emojis:
I don't think you are going to lose your job.
